lesson.title: Logging data you can trust
lesson.subtitle: Plan the log, check the sensor, and clean glitches openly

video.title: Logging data you can trust
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Ms Salma in a classroom holding a phone that shows 85 °C; behind her, pupils at desks in morning light.
scenes.animation: The number 85 flashes red; the head teacher's door swings open.
scenes.narration: Our new classroom sensor said it was eighty-five degrees at seven in the morning. The head teacher nearly sent everyone home. One wrong number almost decided our day. Today: data you can trust.

scenes.visual: Darsi title card with the IoT track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: logging data you can trust.

scenes.visual: A notebook page headed with a question; three answers fill in beneath it: what, where, how often.
scenes.animation: Each line writes itself as it is said.
scenes.narration: Start with a question, not a sensor. Ours: does our classroom get too hot after lunch? So we log the air temperature at desk height, in the shade, every ten minutes.

scenes.visual: A lonely '31' on a card; a unit, a clock and a map pin clip onto it one by one.
scenes.animation: Tags snap on beside the number.
scenes.narration: A reading on its own is just a number. Thirty-one means nothing until you add the unit, degrees Celsius, the time and the place. So: time, unit and place, on every reading.

scenes.visual: The sensor and a glass thermometer side by side on a shelf; two columns of readings fill a page.
scenes.animation: Readings tick in two columns; a '+1' note appears; a wobbly line gets a cross.
scenes.narration: Before you trust a new sensor, check it beside a trusted thermometer, in the same spot, for an hour. If it always reads one degree high, note that and correct for it. If it wanders up and down, don't use it.

scenes.visual: A bar chart of one school day, hour by hour; the 7:00 bar towers over the rest.
scenes.animation: Bars grow left to right; the first bar shoots up and turns red.
scenes.narration: Here's a day from our log. It climbs from twenty-six degrees to thirty-two after lunch. But at seven o'clock: eighty-five. A popular sensor reads exactly that just after it powers up: a classic glitch.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor at his bench pointing at the red 85 bar. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.on_screen_text: What do we do with the 85?
scenes.narration: Quick check! We know the eighty-five is a glitch. What should we do with it?

scenes.visual: Two sheets: the raw log, untouched, and a clean copy with a sticky note on the removed row.
scenes.animation: The sticky note flutters onto the clean copy.
scenes.on_screen_text: Leave it out, and say why
scenes.narration: Leave it out, and write down why. Keep the raw log exactly as it was, and note what you removed: seven o'clock, eighty-five, sensor just powered up. Then anyone can check your cleaning.

scenes.visual: Two boxes side by side: the summary with the glitch, and without it.
scenes.animation: The average jumps from 29 to 36; the median nudges from 29 to 30.
scenes.narration: Why does it matter? With the glitch, the average of those eight readings is about thirty-six degrees, hotter than any real reading. Without it, about twenty-nine. The median, the middle value, is thirty with the glitch and twenty-nine without.

scenes.visual: The eight readings slide into a sorted row; the middle two light up; 30 drops between them.
scenes.animation: Cards shuffle into order; a pointer lands between 29 and 31.
scenes.narration: To find the median, put the readings in order and take the middle one. With an even number, take halfway between the middle two. One wild reading moves it only one place.

scenes.visual: Amina beside a pupil's logbook with two circled readings. Two answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. My pupils' week of readings has two glitches they can't explain. They want one fair number for a typical afternoon: the median, or the average?

scenes.visual: Four icons line up: a question mark, a clock, a scale, a notebook.
scenes.animation: Icons line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: The median: a few wild readings barely move it, but drag the average. Remember: start with a question, put a time, unit and place on every reading, check against a reference, and clean openly.

scenes.visual: A rota pinned by the door; a pupil reads a thermometer and writes a row. The class sorts the readings on the board.
scenes.animation: Rows fill in one by one; the middle value is circled.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: a paper log on a rota. Each hour, a pupil reads a thermometer in the shade and writes the time, reading and unit. Then find the median together. Next time: rules that act on data.

checkpoints.prompt: The log says 85 °C at 7:00, a known glitch. What should we do with that reading?

options.text: Leave it out, and note why

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — leave it out of the summary, keep the raw log, and write down what you removed and why.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — deleting it hides what happened, and keeping it drags the average up. Leave it out, and note why.

checkpoints.prompt: A week of readings has two unexplained glitches. Which gives a fairer typical value?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — two wild readings can drag the average a long way, but the median barely moves.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — wild readings drag the average away from the truth. The median, the middle value, barely moves.
